name: Agomelatine

lead: Agomelatine (Valdoxan) is a prescription antidepressant authorised in the EU since 2009 and in some other countries, but not in the US. Users consider it for its sleep and mood effects, with the hoped-for payoff of lower stress and a fresher, more rested face.

It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors and blocks 5-HT2C receptors, which preclinical work links to increased dopamine and noradrenaline in the frontal cortex. Network meta-analyses have compared it with other antidepressants for major depression; no study has examined appearance.

paras: It is taken by mouth in the evening on prescription for depression, with liver testing as part of use. Mood and sleep effects are judged over weeks.

Reported effects include headache, nausea, dizziness and sleepiness. Raised liver enzymes have been reported, so liver testing is part of use, and it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment. It is not FDA approved.

angle.text: Agomelatine is a melatonin-linked antidepressant that some users consider for sleep and mood, on the theory that better sleep and lower stress show up in the face. It is studied for depression; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Agomelatine is a prescription antidepressant developed by Servier and sold as Valdoxan and Thymanax. It acts as an agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors and a neutral antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C receptors, which makes it the first melatonergic antidepressant.[1][2][3][4] It was authorised in the European Union in 2009 and later in Australia and other countries, but it is not approved by the US FDA.[4]

Its connection to appearance runs through sleep, mood and recovery: depression and disrupted sleep both show in the face and body (tired skin, puffy eyes, lost training consistency), and agomelatine is a drug that targets mood while shifting circadian markers such as sleep phase and melatonin onset in depressed patients.[4] No study has examined it for appearance outcomes, and it is a prescription medicine used for depression and, in Australia, generalised anxiety.[4]

Comparative research includes the 2018 Lancet network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants, which placed agomelatine among the better-tolerated agents, and a 2013 Cochrane review that found it about as effective as other antidepressants.[5][4] Liver enzyme monitoring is part of its prescribing because of reported transaminase rises.[4]

paras: Agomelatine is authorised in the EU for major depressive episodes in adults.[6][4] In Australia it is also approved for generalised anxiety disorder; elsewhere GAD use is off-label, and a 2023 review of anxiety treatment lists agomelatine among agents showing efficacy there.[4][7] It is not recommended in the EU or Australia for people under 18, although a 2022 Lancet Psychiatry trial in ages 7 to 17 reported benefit over placebo, and it is not recommended in dementia, pregnancy or breastfeeding.[4]

Smaller studies have examined agomelatine in circadian rhythm sleep disorders, ADHD with sleep problems, obsessive-compulsive disorder and sleep in obstructive sleep apnoea; these are off-label investigations.[4][8][9][10][11] A 2019 Cochrane review made no recommendation for or against it in seasonal affective disorder.[4]

The 2013 Cochrane review found agomelatine about as effective as other antidepressants with fewer discontinuations because of side effects, and a 2014 meta-analysis of published and unpublished trials reported a standardised mean difference of 0.24 versus standard antidepressants.[4] The 2018 network meta-analysis by Cipriani and colleagues found it comparable to most agents and one of two antidepressants with fewer all-cause discontinuations than placebo.[5][4] A 2007 pooled analysis reported larger drug-placebo differences in severe depression.[4]
Reanalyses have raised concerns about publication bias; Howland (2011) and Koesters (2013) concluded the benefit over placebo was small.[4]

Common effects (1 to 10 percent) include headache, nausea, dizziness, somnolence, diarrhoea, insomnia, fatigue, anxiety and raised liver enzymes, mostly mild and appearing in the first two weeks.[4] Reviews describe a low rate of sexual dysfunction compared with SSRIs and SNRIs, and an Australian review places agomelatine among the antidepressants with the least risk.[12][4][13] Weight change tends to be smaller than with SSRIs, and discontinuation does not require tapering.[4]

Liver safety is the main concern. After Servier's 2012 disclosure to the European Medicines Agency, labelling recommended liver tests before starting, periodically during treatment and after dose changes.[4] A 2016 pooled analysis of 7,605 patients found 36.1 percent of those with raised enzymes normalised without stopping, and a 2019 study found no difference in acute liver injury between agomelatine and citalopram users, a result the article notes may reflect precautionary monitoring.[4] Rare events include mania, suicidal ideation and liver failure. It is contraindicated in hepatic impairment and with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors such as fluvoxamine, and alcohol may increase hepatotoxicity risk.[4]

Agomelatine binds MT1 and MT2 receptors with very high affinity (Ki about 0.1 nM) and is a weak antagonist at 5-HT2C and 5-HT2B receptors.[4] A 2003 preclinical study showed the 5-HT2C blockade enhances frontocortical dopaminergic and noradrenergic activity, giving rise to the label norepinephrine-dopamine disinhibitor.[2][4] Some authors dispute the clinical importance of 5-HT2C antagonism at therapeutic doses, since no human receptor occupancy studies have been done.[4] In depressed patients, agomelatine increases slow-wave sleep and advances sleep phase, the fall in body temperature and melatonin onset.[4]

Absorption is at least 80 percent but bioavailability is about 1 percent because of first-pass metabolism, mainly by CYP1A2 (about 90 percent) and CYP2C9/2C19; half-life is 1 to 2 hours with no accumulation, and about 80 percent is excreted renally as metabolites.[4]
Agomelatine resembles melatonin but replaces the indole ring with a naphthalene bioisostere.[4]

Servier discovered and developed agomelatine; a 2010 Nature Reviews Drug Discovery article describes it as the first melatonergic antidepressant.[3][4] Servier submitted it to the EMA in March 2005 and the CHMP recommended refusal in July 2006 on efficacy grounds; a new application in September 2007 led to EU authorisation in February 2009, and Australia followed in August 2010.[4] Servier licensed US rights to Novartis in 2006, and US development stopped in October 2011 after the final trial results.[4]

Agomelatine is prescription-only in the EU, UK (POM), Australia (S4) and Brazil (Class C1), with low dependence liability.[4] No looksmaxxing community discussion of agomelatine was identified; its presence in this wiki reflects its sleep and circadian mechanism.

Phase 3 placebo-controlled trials in major depression include NCT00411242 (503 participants) and trials of a sublingual formulation, including a 52-week open-label safety study (NCT01156415, 837 participants, terminated).[14][15][16] The 2018 Lancet network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants compared agomelatine with other drugs for acute treatment of adult depression.[5] A 2025 multicentre randomised trial tested agomelatine as an add-on to SSRIs or SNRIs.[17]

Smaller registered trials examined depression with fibromyalgia, cardiovascular effects, depression in schizophrenia and post-stroke depression prevention.[18][19][20] A small placebo-controlled study in ten ADHD patients found agomelatine superior to placebo and less effective than methylphenidate, and a 2025 randomised trial combined electroacupuncture with agomelatine for post-stroke insomnia.[8][21] No studies were found on agomelatine for appearance outcomes.
